q: Under a typical gross lease, which statement is correct?
options: The tenant pays base rent plus its share of property taxes, insurance, and maintenance costs
The tenant pays fixed rent; the landlord pays operating costs like taxes, insurance, and maintenance
The tenant's rent is calculated solely as a percentage of the tenant's gross sales revenue
The tenant leases only the land and constructs and maintains its own building improvements
explanation: In a gross lease the landlord pays the operating expenses out of the rent; it is common for residential and many office leases. Shifting taxes, insurance, and maintenance to the tenant describes a net lease; always read the actual clause for exceptions such as utilities.
citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: A drugstore chain signs a triple net (NNN) lease. Conventionally, this means the tenant pays:
options: Base rent plus property taxes, insurance, and maintenance/repairs
Base rent plus the property taxes only, with the landlord paying the rest
Base rent plus property taxes and insurance only
Only base rent, with the landlord paying all taxes, insurance, and maintenance
explanation: Conventional shorthand: single net = taxes; double net = taxes + insurance; triple net = taxes + insurance + maintenance. The lease language still controls items like roof replacement or capital repairs.
citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: A tenant's lease is described as a double net (net-net) lease. In addition to base rent, the tenant conventionally pays:
options: Property taxes only
Utilities only
Property taxes and insurance
Property taxes, insurance, and maintenance
explanation: Double net conventionally adds taxes and insurance; taxes alone is single net, and adding maintenance makes it triple net. Labels are shorthand only; the clause controls.
citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: A retail lease requires base rent of $3,000 per month plus 4% of annual gross sales over $600,000. The tenant's gross sales this year were $850,000. What is the total annual rent?
citation: Commercial leasing principles — percentage lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: A percentage lease has annual base rent of $60,000 and percentage rent of 6% of gross sales. Assuming a natural breakpoint, at what level of annual gross sales does percentage rent begin?
explanation: Natural breakpoint = annual base rent ÷ percentage rate = $60,000 ÷ 0.06 = $1,000,000. Above that, 6% of sales exceeds the base rent. A lease may instead set a negotiated (artificial) breakpoint.
citation: Commercial leasing principles — percentage lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: A boutique's percentage lease requires 5% of gross sales over a breakpoint. Sales exceeded the breakpoint, but the owner tells the landlord no percentage rent is owed because the store lost money this year. Is the owner correct?
options: No, percentage rent is based on gross sales, not on profit
Yes, percentage rent is owed only when the tenant shows a net profit
Yes, a loss year automatically suspends percentage rent
No, percentage rent is based on the landlord's operating expenses
explanation: Percentage rent is computed on defined gross sales above the breakpoint, regardless of whether the tenant's business is profitable. These leases are most common for retail tenants in shopping centers.
citation: Commercial leasing principles — percentage lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: An index lease sets annual rent at $80,000 when the Consumer Price Index is 250. The rent adjusts by the full percentage change in the CPI, with no cap. If the CPI rises to 260, what is the new annual rent?
explanation: CPI change = (260 − 250) ÷ 250 = 10 ÷ 250 = 4%. New rent = $80,000 × 1.04 = $83,200. Treating the 10-point rise as 10 percent or adding points to the rent are the traps.
citation: Commercial leasing principles — index lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: An office lease sets rent at $30 per square foot in year 1, $32 in year 2, and $34 in year 3, as written in the lease from the start. This is a:
options: Index lease
Percentage lease
Net lease
Graduated lease
explanation: A graduated (step-up) lease raises rent by fixed, pre-set amounts on a schedule. An index lease instead moves rent with an outside measure such as the CPI, so the future amounts are not known in advance.
citation: Commercial leasing principles — graduated lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: A fast-food chain leases a vacant parcel for 49 years and constructs its own restaurant on it. This arrangement is best described as a:
options: Ground lease
Gross lease
Percentage lease
Graduated lease
explanation: A ground lease is a long-term lease of land only, with the tenant building and usually paying expenses on the improvements. Unless the lease provides otherwise, the improvements commonly pass to the landowner when the lease ends.
citation: Commercial leasing principles — ground lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: In an office building, how does rentable square footage differ from usable square footage?
options: Rentable area excludes the lobbies and corridors that are included in usable area
Rentable area adds the tenant's pro-rata share of common areas like lobbies and restrooms
Rentable and usable area are always identical; the terms are interchangeable in office leases
Rentable area counts only the finished space with carpeting and ceilings installed
explanation: Usable area is the space the tenant actually occupies; rentable area adds its share of building common areas. Rent is usually quoted per rentable square foot, so rentable is the larger number.
citation: Commercial leasing principles — area measurement; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: A suite has 10,000 rentable square feet and 8,500 usable square feet. What is the loss factor?
explanation: Loss factor = (rentable − usable) ÷ rentable = 1,500 ÷ 10,000 = 15%. Dividing by usable (1,500 ÷ 8,500 ≈ 17.6%) gives the add-on/load percentage instead, and 85% is the efficiency (usable ÷ rentable).
citation: Commercial leasing principles — loss factor; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: A tenant needs 4,000 usable square feet. The building has a 20% add-on (load) factor applied to usable area, and rent is $45 per rentable square foot per year. What is the monthly rent?
explanation: Rentable = 4,000 × 1.20 = 4,800 sq ft. Annual rent = 4,800 × $45 = $216,000; monthly = $216,000 ÷ 12 = $18,000. Using usable area (4,000 × $45 ÷ 12 = $15,000) ignores the load.
citation: Commercial leasing principles — load factor; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: A tenant occupies 3,000 square feet in a 60,000-square-foot shopping center. Annual common area maintenance (CAM) costs are $240,000, shared pro rata by square footage. What is the tenant's annual CAM charge?
explanation: Pro-rata share = 3,000 ÷ 60,000 = 5%. CAM = $240,000 × 0.05 = $12,000 per year ($1,000 per month). CAM is a cost-sharing charge for common areas such as parking lots and landscaping, not a measurement of space.
citation: Commercial leasing principles — CAM charges; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: A lease provides a tenant improvement (TI) allowance of $40 per rentable square foot on 5,000 rentable square feet. The tenant's build-out costs $260,000, and the lease says the tenant pays any excess. How much does the tenant pay toward the build-out?
explanation: TI allowance = $40 × 5,000 = $200,000 paid by the landlord. Tenant pays the excess: $260,000 − $200,000 = $60,000. TI allowances are a negotiated landlord concession to customize space.
citation: Commercial leasing principles — tenant improvements; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: An investor buys a building with $350,000 cash invested. NOI is $120,000 and annual debt service is $85,000. What is the investor's cash-on-cash return?
explanation: Before-tax cash flow = NOI − debt service = $120,000 − $85,000 = $35,000. Cash-on-cash = $35,000 ÷ $350,000 = 10%. Dividing NOI by cash invested (34.3%) skips debt service.
citation: Real estate investment analysis; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: An investor finances a purchase mostly with borrowed money. Positive leverage occurs when:
options: The loan's interest rate is higher than the property's rate of return
The investor pays all cash so no debt service is owed
The property's NOI is less than the annual debt service
The property's rate of return exceeds the cost of the borrowed funds
explanation: Leverage uses borrowed money to increase the return on the investor's own cash. It is positive when the property earns more than the debt costs; if the debt costs more, leverage is negative and magnifies losses.
citation: Real estate investment analysis; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: A building listed at $1,100,000 has gross scheduled income of $96,000, operating expenses of $30,000, and annual mortgage payments of $40,000. What is the capitalization rate at the list price?
explanation: NOI = $96,000 − $30,000 = $66,000 (mortgage payments are not operating expenses). Cap rate = NOI ÷ price = $66,000 ÷ $1,100,000 = 6%. Using gross income (8.7%) or deducting debt service (2.4%) are traps.
citation: Real estate investment analysis — capitalization rate; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

q: In an ordinary deferred Section 1031 exchange, after the relinquished property is transferred, the investor must identify replacement property and then receive it within what time limits?
options: Identify within 45 days; receive within 180 days or by the tax-return due date, if earlier
Identify within 30 days; receive within 90 days or by the tax-return due date, if earlier
Identify within 60 days; receive within 120 days of closing on the relinquished property
Identify within 45 days; receive within one year
explanation: Replacement property must be identified in writing within 45 days and received by the earlier of 180 days after the transfer or the tax-return due date (with extensions). A qualified intermediary should hold the proceeds so the investor never receives them.

q: An investor exchanges a rental building for a larger warehouse under Section 1031 and also receives $40,000 in cash. The $40,000 is:
options: Like-kind property, so it is fully tax-deferred
A qualified intermediary fee deductible as an expense
Boot, generally taxable up to the amount of realized gain
Excluded from tax because the exchange was between real properties
explanation: Cash or other non-like-kind property received is boot and can trigger taxable gain up to the realized gain. A rental building for a warehouse is like-kind because both are investment/business real property; a personal home does not qualify.

q: A salesperson represents a buyer of a 20,000-square-foot warehouse in New York. Which statement about required disclosure forms is correct?
options: Both the RPL § 443 agency disclosure form and the fair housing and discrimination notice are required
Neither form is required because commercial transactions are exempt from all DOS notices
Only the RPL § 443 agency disclosure form is required
The RPL § 443 agency disclosure form is not required, but the fair housing and discrimination notice is
explanation: The RPL § 443 agency disclosure form covers residential (1-4 family, condo, co-op) transactions, so it does not apply to a warehouse. The DOS Fair Housing and Discrimination notice under 19 NYCRR § 175.28 applies to all real property, including commercial and vacant land.
citation: NY RPL § 443; 19 NYCRR § 175.28

q: A restaurant tenant wants to lease space in a zoning district where restaurants are allowed only if the zoning board finds that specified conditions in the ordinance (parking, hours, traffic) are met. The tenant should apply for a:
options: Use variance
Special use permit
Nonconforming use designation
Spot zoning amendment
explanation: A special use permit (special exception) allows a use the ordinance already permits subject to stated conditions. A use variance is needed for a use the ordinance prohibits and requires proof of unnecessary hardship.
citation: NY Town Law § 274-b; NY Village Law § 7-725-b

q: A retail tenant's lease says the tenant is solely responsible for ADA compliance. A customer who uses a wheelchair cannot enter the store because of steps at the entrance. Under ADA Title III, who may be responsible to the public?
options: Only the tenant, because the lease validly shifted all ADA compliance responsibility to it
Only the landlord, because it owns the building and controls the common entrance and steps
Both the landlord and the tenant; the lease allocates the burden but does not erase either's duty
Neither, because ADA Title III applies only to residential housing
explanation: Title III covers public accommodations such as stores, and both the landlord and the tenant can be liable; a lease can allocate the burden between them but cannot waive duties owed to the public. Existing facilities must remove barriers where readily achievable.
citation: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III, 42 U.S.C. § 12181 et seq.; 28 CFR § 36.201(b)
